claims.text: The target MPEA is brittle at room temperature in its cast or standard-annealed state.
The initial alloy has coarse grains and low dislocation density.
Restricted slip activity causes the alloy's limited room-temperature ductility.
Severe plastic deformation will introduce a high density of dislocations.
Severe plastic deformation will refine the grain structure.
A short anneal below the solvus and above the recovery temperature will nucleate nanoscale precipitates.
An appropriate short annealing interval can avoid significant grain growth and precipitate coarsening.
The treatment will produce a heavily deformed, ultrafine-grained matrix.
The treated microstructure will contain a high density of nanoscale coherent precipitates.
The treated microstructure will contain a gradient of geometrically necessary dislocations.
The resulting microstructure will be dual-phase.
The nanoscale precipitates will increase yield strength through Orowan strengthening.
The GND population and refined grains will promote strain hardening.
Grain-boundary sliding and GND-mediated strain hardening will delay necking and enhance tensile ductility.
The non-equilibrium processing state will prevent brittle intermetallic phases associated with standard thermal treatments.
The route will activate multiple slip systems.
Yield strength will increase by more than 20% relative to the initial state.
Tensile ductility will increase by more than 15% relative to the initial state.
Standard solution annealing, slow cooling, or aging typically produces either high strength with low ductility or high ductility with low strength in standard MPEAs.
The proposed route is applicable to moderate-stacking-fault-energy MPEAs in which nanoscale precipitation is thermodynamically feasible but kinetically hindered during standard processing.
